Write methods that each reliably finish with a high-precision answer. Use a multistart-plus-polish structure: spend about 70% of the optimiser calls on many cheap, diverse starts, then spend the rest on tight-tolerance polishing of the best 1-3 candidates. Make the starts structured, not uniform random. Examples are hexagonal or square lattices with a few points removed or shifted, concentric rings, and symmetric layouts. Add small perturbations of the incumbent, such as moving the worst-placed element or swapping a pair. Keep the best feasible result in memory and never return anything worse. Across the four methods, vary the start generator and the move type, and keep each method's budget logic sound. Stop early on a method that fails, and always return a feasible solution.

Treat this as global search over many local minima, where the best known value is probably a particular structured basin. Write methods that explore basins quickly and then exploit the best one. Use basin hopping or iterated local search: run the optimiser, apply a structured kick (shift a row, rotate a ring, remove the tightest element and reinsert it in the largest gap, or mirror a half), re-optimise, and accept improvements. Seed from lattice, ring and symmetric configurations suited to the problem's shape. Give each method a different kick type and a different seed family. Reserve the last 15% of calls for a final polish with tight tolerances and active-constraint handling. Always return the best feasible point found.

Mix safe and exploratory methods so that at least two of the four are dependable. The dependable ones are a well-tuned multistart from lattice or symmetric seeds with a final high-accuracy polish, and a continuation scheme that starts from a relaxed or penalised problem and tightens it, with the last stage solved exactly. The other two should try one different structural idea each, such as exploiting symmetry to cut the variables, growing the configuration one element at a time and re-optimising, or removing and reinserting the worst element. Plan the call budget explicitly: how many calls go to exploration, how many to refinement, and when to stop. Verify feasibility and keep the best result.

Write four methods that differ in core idea, not parameters: (1) many structured starts, each a local solve; (2) basin hopping with structured kicks; (3) continuation from a penalised or softened problem, such as a soft-min or a growing radius, tightened step by step; (4) a reduced-variable method that exploits symmetry or a row or ring structure. Give every method a cheap exploration phase, then a final polish. The polish identifies the active constraints, fixes them as equalities, and re-solves with very tight tolerances (ftol about 1e-15) so the answer is accurate to many digits. Keep the best feasible point seen, and never return a worse or infeasible one. Spend roughly 75% of the calls on exploration and the rest on polishing the top 2 candidates. Stop each method early when the budget is gone.

The best known value is almost certainly a precise, structured local optimum, so near-misses score poorly. Reaching the right basin matters, and so does converging fully inside it. Write methods that each pair a different basin-finding idea with an exact finish. Basin-finding ideas: perturbed hexagonal or square lattices with a few elements removed, concentric rings with varied counts per ring, greedy insertion into the largest gap, and random starts that are shrunk and re-expanded. The exact finish takes the best 2-3 candidates and re-runs the optimiser from each with tight tolerances. It repeats until the objective stops improving in the 12th digit, and treats constraints within 1e-9 of active as active. Plan the budget so the finish always gets at least 20% of the calls. Return the best feasible point, with a feasibility check before returning.

Propose methods that differ from each other and from the ones above in their core idea, not in parameters. Prefer ideas that reach different basins: different symmetry classes, different row or ring counts, different insertion orders, and different relaxations of the constraints. Make each method self-contained and robust: every optimiser call sits in try/except, the best feasible result is tracked throughout, and the call count is checked before each call. Each method must end by re-optimising its best point with tight tolerances so the digits converge. Within each method, spend more calls on diverse starts than on repeats of the same start. Always return a feasible solution.

Propose four methods whose core ideas differ, and avoid repeating the ones above. Each method should enumerate a different discrete structure family, not sample random starts. Examples are ring-count compositions (such as 1-6-12-7), hexagonal row counts and offsets, square or rectangular grids with k elements removed, and mirror or rotational symmetry classes. Screen every candidate with a cheap, low-iteration solve and rank them. Fully converge only the best 2-3, using tight tolerances. Then repeat the optimiser from the result until the 12th digit stops changing. Check the call count before every call, wrap each call in try/except, and keep the best feasible point throughout. Across methods, vary the family, the screening relaxation (for example a growing radius or a soft penalty), and the insertion order. Reserve at least 25% of the calls for the final convergence. The target is a precise structured optimum, so the method must find the right basin and then converge fully. Write four methods with different basin-finding ideas. (1) A lattice sweep: hexagonal and square lattices at several orientations, with every choice of removed elements or shifted rows. (2) Concentric rings with systematically varied counts per ring. (3) Greedy gap insertion, followed by remove-the-tightest-and-reinsert moves. (4) Basin hopping from the incumbent, with structured kicks such as a row shift, a ring rotation, or swapping two elements. Use cheap solves to explore, keep a pool of the 3 best distinct candidates, and spend the last 25% of calls on tight-tolerance re-solves of that pool. Treat constraints within 1e-9 of active as active. Stop when the objective changes by less than 1e-13. Never return an infeasible or worse point.

Make the four methods complementary. Two should be dependable: a structured multistart (lattice, ring and symmetric seeds, with varied counts) and a continuation method that tightens a relaxed problem. Two should be exploratory and each try a different basin-changing idea, such as a different symmetry class, a different row or ring layout, or growing the configuration one element at a time. Allocate calls explicitly. Use about 60% on diverse starts, 15% on perturbing the incumbent (move the worst element to the largest gap), and 25% on polishing the top 2 candidates with very tight tolerances. Do not spend calls repeating a start that has already converged. Check the budget before each call, catch exceptions, and track the best feasible result. Always return a feasible point.
